coverageDimensions:
SERVICE coverage would mean: of the AWS services in existence, how many have at least one resource type that RAM can share. The page gives you the numerator directly and cleanly — 41 owning services, one per H2 heading, from AWS App Mesh to Amazon VPC Lattice. It gives you no denominator: nothing here enumerates the AWS services RAM cannot share from. Treat 41 as a derived rollup of the resource-type axis, not as a second capability, because the service headings are grouping furniture and every claim on the page is actually made about a resource type.

RESOURCE TYPE coverage would mean: of all AWS resource types, how many RAM can share. This is the page's native axis and its strongest contribution — 84 codes in 83 rows, each written in `service:Type` form, so the values are machine-clean and need no normalisation. Again numerator only. The AWS resource-type universe runs to several thousand entries; this page names 84 of them and is silent on every other one. Absence is the only way a type is excluded, and absence is not an assertion — never render an unlisted type as an explicit "not supported" sourced to this page.

REGION coverage would mean: in which AWS Regions RAM can share a given resource type. The page gives you nothing. The word Region appears once, incidentally, inside the AWS AppSync use-case prose ("across different accounts in the same Region"), which is a description of merged-API behaviour and not a coverage statement. There is no Region column, no Region table, no per-Region availability note, and no link to a Region table. Any Region claim attributed to this page would be fabricated.

What the page does give beyond those three is a fourth dimension the standard trio misses: sharing target. Four of them — accounts (the implicit baseline), IAM users and roles, accounts outside the organization, and AWS service principals — each with its own Yes/No split, plus a permission-model dimension (AWS managed always, customer managed for 46 of 83). A coverage map that only records "RAM supports 84 resource types" throws away the four splits that carry the security signal.

features.reasoning: AWS resource types are an external universe: `ec2:Subnet`, `glue:Table` and `sagemaker:Pipeline` exist whether or not RAM shares them, and the great majority of AWS resource types are absent from this page. That makes the ratio real and meaningful — RAM reaches 84 resource types out of the far larger AWS resource-type universe — even though this page supplies only the numerator. It is emphatically not a catalogue: RAM does not mint these types, other services do, and RAM's own list is the short one.
features.scope: Grouped by owning AWS service — 41 service sections
features.statuses: 84 supported, 0 not-supported. Every code on the page is, by the page's own framing ("You can share the following <service> resources by using AWS RAM"), a supported type. There is no not-supported half on this axis: exclusion is expressed by absence, not by a No. The four Yes/No columns qualify HOW a supported type can be shared; they never mark a type as unshareable. 84 codes sit in 83 table rows because the AWS Network Firewall row "Network Firewall Rule groups" carries two codes, `network-firewall:StatefulRuleGroup` and `network-firewall:StatelessRuleGroup`.

features.featureName: Can share with IAM users and roles
features.reasoning: A distinct capability with its own supported/not-supported split over the same resource-type axis, so it must be extracted separately from the row list. Count is 83 statements, not 84, because the verdict is asserted once per row and the Network Firewall rule-groups row covers two codes with one verdict — the row is the unit of assertion here. Whether to project that verdict onto both codes is a modelling choice the page does not make for you.
features.scope: Per resource type; matrix column 3 of the per-service tables
features.statuses: 44 Yes, 39 No. Stated by an explicit Yes/No column with icon-yes.png / icon-no.png images beside the word. Legend: Yes = shareable with individual IAM roles and users in addition to accounts; No = shareable with accounts only.

features.featureName: Can share with accounts outside its organization
features.reasoning: A separate security-relevant capability: it is the page's only statement about cross-organization reach, which is exactly the blast-radius question a security coverage map cares about. It has a genuine No population, unlike the row axis. The single conditional cell must be carried as conditional, not collapsed to Yes or No, because collapsing it either invents cross-org sharing for Capacity Blocks or denies it for Capacity Reservations.
features.scope: Per resource type; matrix column 4 of the per-service tables
features.statuses: 68 Yes, 14 No, 1 conditional. The 14 No rows are the real exclusions on this page: `bedrock:CustomModel`, `billing:billingview`, `servicediscovery:Namespace`, `odb:CloudExadataInfrastructure`, `odb:OdbNetwork`, `outposts:Outpost`, `ec2:LocalGatewayRouteTable`, `s3-outposts:Outpost`, `resource-explorer-2:View`, `servicecatalog:Applications`, `servicecatalog:AttributeGroups`, `ec2:CoipPool`, `ec2:Subnet`, `ec2:SecurityGroup` — each reading "No — Can share with only AWS accounts in its own organization". The conditional is Amazon EC2 `ec2:CapacityReservation`: "Yes for Capacity Reservations (any AWS account). No for Capacity Blocks (only AWS accounts in its own organization)." — one cell, two verdicts, no icon. Of the 68 Yes, 65 add "Can share with any AWS account" and 3 are a bare Yes.

features.reasoning: Separate column, separate Yes/No split, separate meaning — permission model, not sharing target. The legend sentence is load-bearing and must travel with the extraction; without it a No in this column reads as an absence of permission support, which is wrong.
features.scope: Per resource type; matrix column 5 of the per-service tables
features.statuses: 46 Yes, 37 No. The legend qualifies the meaning: "All resource types supported by AWS RAM support AWS managed permissions, but a Yes in this column means that customer managed permissions is also supported for this resource type." So a No here means customer managed permissions is unavailable, not that the type is unsupported by RAM.

features.reasoning: The sparsest and therefore the most easily mis-transcribed column, and a distinct sharing target (an AWS service principal, not an account or an IAM principal). Its 5/78 split is the clearest evidence on the page that each column is its own capability rather than a decoration of the row.
features.scope: Per resource type; matrix column 6 of the per-service tables
features.statuses: 5 Yes, 78 No. The five Yes rows are `sms-voice:PhoneNumber`, `sms-voice:Pool`, `sms-voice:SenderId` (AWS End User Messaging SMS), `acm-pca:CertificateAuthority` (AWS Private Certificate Authority), and `s3:AccessGrants` (Amazon Simple Storage Service). Legend: Yes = you can share resources of this type with AWS services; No = you can't.

features.reasoning: A real coverage claim of the required shape, and it must be recorded so the customer-managed-permissions column is not read as the whole permissions story. Flag it as universal-by-statement and derived from prose, not from a column: it carries no discriminating information across the axis and should never be charted as a 100% score.
features.scope: Stated in the legend as a blanket rule, not as a table column
features.statuses: 84 supported, 0 not-supported, from one prose sentence: "All resource types supported by AWS RAM support AWS managed permissions". There is no column for it and no per-row evidence.

shouldNotExtract:
The four-row legend table at the top (lines 11-16): its left cells are the four column names and its right cells are the Yes/No definitions. It has an empty header row and no resource codes, and a parser that treats every pipe-table as a data table will emit "Can share with IAM users and roles" as a shareable resource type. Read it once for semantics, extract nothing from it.

The "Use case" column in every row — free prose plus deep links into 40-odd other AWS user guides. It is rationale, not enumeration; none of its named features (merged APIs, multicast domains, Verified Access endpoints) are coverage values.

The repeated sentence "You can share the following <service> resources by using AWS RAM" (41 copies) — boilerplate section lead-in.

The 41 H2 service headings as capability values. They are the grouping key for the resource-type axis, usable as a derived service rollup, never as the primary value set.

The `<a name="shareable">` / `<a name="permissions-rbp-supported-resource-types">` anchors and every per-section anchor; the icon image URLs (icon-yes.png / icon-no.png), which are the verdict's carrier but not content; and the markdown separator rows.

The whole "See also" section, whose sole bullet is the AI-coding-assistants boilerplate AWS now appends to every page ("Skills for AI coding assistants (optional)... aws agent-toolkit search-skills --search-query ram"). It is not a capability, not a value, and not a link to a coverage table.
trap:
The single likeliest mistake is flattening the matrix — taking the 83 rows as one list called "resource types RAM supports" and dropping the four Yes/No columns, or worse, folding them into one boolean. That destroys the only security-relevant content: that 39 of 83 types cannot be shared with IAM users and roles, that 14 cannot leave the organization, and that only 5 can be shared with AWS service principals.

Close behind it, in rough order of likelihood:

Counting rows and calling them codes. 83 rows carry 84 codes; the AWS Network Firewall row "Network Firewall Rule groups" lists `network-firewall:StatefulRuleGroup` and `network-firewall:StatelessRuleGroup` in one cell under one shared set of verdicts. A regex that grabs the first backticked token per row silently loses the stateless rule group.

Collapsing the one conditional cell. Amazon EC2 `ec2:CapacityReservation` under "Can share with accounts outside its organization" reads "Yes for Capacity Reservations... No for Capacity Blocks..." with no icon image at all. An icon-driven parser returns null and may default it to No; a text-driven parser matches the leading "Yes" and grants Capacity Blocks a cross-organization reach the page explicitly denies.

Reading "Can use customer managed permissions: No" as "RAM does not support permissions for this type". The legend says every supported type gets AWS managed permissions; the No is narrower than it looks.

Publishing a ratio with the wrong denominator — "RAM covers 82% for cross-organization sharing" (68/83) sounds like coverage of AWS but is only a split within RAM's own 84 types. The true resource-type denominator, the AWS resource-type universe, is not on this page and must come from elsewhere or be left blank.

Mistaking absence for a No. An unlisted type such as `dynamodb:Table` is not asserted unsupported here; it is simply unmentioned.

Finally, the second anchor `permissions-rbp-supported-resource-types` invites the reading that this is a list of resource types supporting resource-based policies. It is not — it is the RAM shareable-types list, and the anchor is a historical redirect.
whatThePageStates: This is the AWS RAM user guide's master list of which AWS resource types can be shared through AWS Resource Access Manager. After a short intro and a four-row legend, the page runs 41 H2 sections, one per owning AWS service (AWS App Mesh through Amazon VPC Lattice), each containing one table. Every table has identical columns: "Resource type and code" (a display name plus a `service:Type` code), "Use case" (prose), and four Yes/No capability columns — "Can share with IAM users and roles", "Can share with accounts outside its organization", "Can use customer managed permissions", "Can share with service principals". Across all 41 tables there are 83 resource-type rows carrying 84 distinct resource-type codes. This is a matrix page: the row axis is one capability (what RAM can share at all) and each of the four Yes/No columns is a separate capability measured over that same axis.
